strengths: Rigorous unifying theoretical framework that elegantly connects noise-expectation and gradient-expectation families of existing methods through a common posterior mean estimation lens, with detailed mappings in Appendix B

Sound mathematical development with correct theorems, propositions, and proofs establishing equivalence between RFM and CFM, decomposition properties, and variance-minimizing control variate coefficients
Novel application of Langevin Stein operators to construct zero-mean control variates for online RL, principled combination of Q-value and Q-gradient information
Extends framework beyond diffusion policies to flow policies with greater flexibility through non-Gaussian source distributions
Consistent empirical improvements across 8 DMC environments and practical algorithm (Algorithm 1) that is implementable
weaknesses: Limited experimental validation: Only 8 DMC environments tested; missing ablation studies to validate key theoretical claims (e.g., empirical variance reduction from control variates, sensitivity to η, effect of N samples); overlapping error bars in several tasks undermine claims of 'substantially better stability'

Theory-practice gap: Theorem 1's mutual absolute continuity assumption between pt and pˆt is stated abstractly but may not hold when Xt is sampled from replay buffer; assumption of sufficiently rich function class is unrealistic for neural networks; finite-dimensional approximation of optimal test functions (Eq. 15) lacks error analysis

Incomplete technical analysis: No computational cost comparison despite adding SNIS overhead; missing discussion of proposal mismatch effects; non-Gaussian source extension (Appendix A) lacks experimental validation; practical details sparse (what N, tmin, λ sensitivity?)

Presentation issues: Heavy mathematical content without sufficient intuition for reverse inference perspective; notation overloading (β); abrupt transition to Langevin Stein operators lacking motivation; experimental section (1.5 pages) too brief with insufficient implementation details

Modest empirical improvements with statistical significance unclear due to overlapping confidence intervals in multiple environments; no evidence method solves critical limitations of existing approaches; applicability beyond continuous control unexplored

strengths: Novel reverse flow matching perspective that elegantly reframes unavailable target samples as a posterior mean estimation problem
Rigorous mathematical development with sound theorems and propositions, particularly the Langevin Stein operator construction for variance reduction
Valuable unification showing noise-expectation and gradient-expectation methods as special cases (η=0 vs η=1), providing conceptual clarity
Technical soundness of control variate derivations with explicit formulas for optimal coefficients (Propositions 4-5)
Extension of framework from diffusion to flow policies with principled variance reduction
weaknesses: Experimental validation is insufficient: Figure 1 lacks quantitative comparisons, confidence intervals overlap substantially, no ablations demonstrating value of control variates or which components drive improvements

Critical implementation details are missing or unclear: proposal distribution p̂_t choice in practice, computational cost of optimal Λ coefficient computation, hyperparameter sensitivity (t_min, N, etc.)
Theory-practice gap: Theorem 1 requires 'sufficiently rich' function class achieving global minima, but neural networks achieve only local minima; practical implications unaddressed
Unclear which aspects drive performance gains: no ablation isolating framework vs. variance reduction vs. flow policies; no experiments validating claimed benefits of flexible source distributions
Limited practical guidance: no clear characterization of when RFM is preferred over baselines; claims like 'consistently better' lack statistical significance testing
Remark 6 pragmatic compromise (using standard Q-function instead of soft Q-function) suggests computational constraints that undermine the maximum entropy RL framing
Baseline comparison concerns: all reimplemented for 'fair comparison' without clear validation; no comparison with recent flow-based methods [11,18,22]
Missing key ablations: (1) RFM framework contribution alone, (2) empirical impact of optimal coefficient selection (η=0 vs η=1 vs optimal), (3) flow vs. diffusion using same RFM framework

strengths: Novel reverse inference perspective elegantly reformulates unavailable target samples as posterior mean estimation, with clean mathematical derivations (Propositions 1, Theorem 1)
Principled application of Langevin Stein operators to construct variance-reducing control variates, with explicit optimal coefficient formulas (Propositions 4-5)
Meaningful unification showing noise-expectation and gradient-expectation families are special cases (η=0 and η=1), providing conceptual clarity through Appendix B
Rigorous mathematical framework with sound proofs (Theorem 2 characterizing Boltzmann case is particularly elegant)
Extends capability to flow policies beyond diffusion, offering greater flexibility through general source distributions
Demonstrates consistent stability across 8 continuous-control environments where each baseline struggles on some tasks
Well-motivated problem: training expressive policies on Boltzmann-distributed targets is important for online RL
weaknesses: Critical assumption in Theorem 1 that p̂t and pt are mutually absolutely continuous is insufficiently justified; the gradient difference (∇LRFM ≠ ∇LCFM except when p̂t=pt) could affect optimization dynamics but implications are not discussed

No empirical ablation studies on design choices: impact of η parameter (Q-value vs Q-gradient trade-off), effect of control variates on variance reduction, sensitivity to SNIS sample size N, or choices like tmin are all unexplored

Proposal distribution p₀=N(0,I) for Boltzmann posteriors appears arbitrary; no justification for this choice over learned proposals; importance weights w∝exp(Q/λ) could have unbounded variance for large Q-ranges—fundamental stability issues unaddressed

Empirical improvements in Figure 1 are modest and could reflect implementation details; claim of being 'only algorithm performing consistently well' is overstated given overlapping confidence intervals and modest differences; no statistical significance testing reported

Missing experimental details preventing reproducibility: test function initialization, λ selection procedure, network architectures unspecified, only 5 seeds per task, no wall-clock time or computational cost comparisons despite acknowledged extra ∇Q computation

Computing ∇Q(s,a) for control variate term (Eq. 23) doubles backpropagation cost vs pure Q-methods; this computational overhead is mentioned but not quantified or justified against the modest empirical gains
Boundary and regularity conditions for Langevin Stein operators (Lemmas 2-3) are assumed but not verified to hold for the Boltzmann+Gaussian setting; no discussion of failure modes in practice
No analysis of how importance weights behave as Q-estimates change during RL training; early training when Q-estimates are poor could yield unstable SNIS estimators, but this is not addressed

strengths: Rigorous theoretical framework with elegant reverse inference perspective that converts unavailable target samples into tractable posterior mean estimation problem
Novel unification of noise-expectation and gradient-expectation methods as special cases of parametric family (Eq. 21), with detailed recovery of prior methods in Appendix B
Sound use of generalized Langevin Stein operators (Definition 4.6, Propositions 4.7-4.10) to construct variance-reducing control variates through learned coefficients
Extension of Boltzmann distribution targeting from diffusion to flow policies, enabling greater flexibility through general source distributions
Comprehensive experimental validation including toy examples, 8 DMC environments, ablation studies (Section G.2), and sensitivity analyses with consistent stability improvements across diverse tasks
Well-written with clear exposition, strong mathematical development, comprehensive related works categorization, and helpful appendices (especially Appendix B mapping prior methods)
weaknesses: Strong theoretical assumptions (mutual absolute continuity in Theorem 4.2, 'sufficiently rich' function class) lack practical justification; unclear how violations affect performance in finite-capacity networks or when proposal support is smaller than target

Incomplete computational cost analysis: (1) ∇Q computation for control variates adds unquantified overhead, (2) Table 2 shows 1.5-4× training time vs. baselines without justifying modest empirical gains, (3) variance reduction benefit per unit computation not analyzed

Circular dependency in variance optimization: Proposition 4.9 estimates optimal Λ* from same samples used for posterior mean estimation (Eq. 15), raising potential overfitting and correlation issues that deserve theoretical analysis

Limited experimental scope: only 8 DMC environments, 2D toy example too simple for scalability assessment, missing evaluation on vision-based/manipulation tasks where generative policies excel, no failure mode analysis

Design-theory mismatch: framework targets soft Q-function with entropy but RFM uses standard Q-function for computational convenience; ablation (Figure 4) shows this improves performance, contradicting motivation
Modest empirical improvements despite higher computational cost (Figure 2 shows ~50-100 reward differences); statistical significance testing absent and practical utility unclear for practitioners
Hyperparameter sensitivity unexplored: λ = 0.02 fixed across all environments, K=100 for SNIS appears arbitrary, ridge term r in Λ estimation is heuristic without justification

Practical algorithm details unclear: Algorithm 1 is sparse, connection between theoretical sections (4.1-4.2) and instantiation (4.4) underdeveloped, choice of linear schedule (α_t=t, β_t=1-t) late with no sensitivity analysis
